paragraphs.text: Oocyte/zygote/embryo maturation arrest-26 (OZEMA26) is a form of female primary infertility. It is marked by early embryonic arrest and implantation failure during assisted reproduction cycles (Dong et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2026). Embryos from affected women have shown extensive aneuploidy (Wu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Some patients have shown abnormal fertilization with multiple pronuclei (Jiao et al., 2025).

Screening of patients with embryonic arrest, recurrent implantation failure, and recurrent pregnancy loss identified 7 further patients from 6 families. In these patients, biallelic MEI1 mutations were associated with early embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure.

paragraphs.text: Jiao et al. (2025) reported 2 unrelated Chinese women with embryonic developmental arrest. They were identified among 20 women with a high rate of abnormal fertilization during ICSI at a center in Guangzhou, China. The first proband was a 32-year-old woman with a 4-year history of primary infertility. She had regular menstrual cycles and a normal ovarian reserve. Eight of her ICSI-fertilized oocytes became 3PN or PPN embryos. Of her IVF-fertilized oocytes, 5 showed normal 2PN formation and 3 became 3PN/PPN embryos. None of the 2PN-derived embryos from conventional IVF formed blastocysts. In contrast, 2 of 3 3PN/PPN-derived embryos from ICSI developed into late-stage blastocysts. Her sister had normal fertility. The second proband was a 35-year-old woman with an 8-year history of primary infertility and normal ovarian function. She had 2 unsuccessful IVF cycles before her third, ICSI, cycle. In that cycle, 3 oocytes became normal 2PN embryos and 1 became a 1PN embryo. Two of 3 viable frozen embryos were transferred, but neither resulted in pregnancy. Jiao et al. (2025) noted that the 3PN/PPN embryos reached the blastocyst stage. They suggested that in natural pregnancies such embryos might implant and develop into hydatidiform moles.

paragraphs.text: In a study of 9 women with primary infertility from 7 families, Dong et al. (2021) used whole-exome sequencing with Sanger confirmation to identify 5 novel MEI1 mutations. Some patients had recurrent hydatidiform moles, and others had early embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure. In those with embryonic arrest or implantation failure, the mutations were biallelic. Western blotting showed that protein-truncating and missense mutations reduced MEI1 protein levels. Minigene analysis showed that splicing mutations caused abnormal alternative splicing of MEI1.

paragraphs.text: In a consanguineous family, Liu et al. (2025) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous deletion of MEI1 exon 19. Carriers were a man with azoospermia and a woman with embryonic arrest. Their mother was a heterozygous carrier. Sequencing of cDNA confirmed loss of the whole exon, and patients had almost no detectable expression of exon 19. In transfected HEK293T cells, western blotting showed that the deletion produced a truncated MEI1 protein. This was consistent with the predicted premature termination in exon 20.

paragraphs.text: Jiao et al. (2025) used whole-exome sequencing to find compound heterozygous MEI1 variants in 2 unrelated women with embryonic developmental arrest. The first woman carried S208P and R883X. The second carried W1013G together with a deletion of exons 21 to 31. Because that deletion includes position c.3037, the second woman appeared homozygous for the c.3037T-G change on sequencing. The deletion was confirmed by qPCR. In transfected HEK293T cells, R883X reduced MEI1 protein levels and W1013G increased them. S208P and the exon 21-31 deletion did not change protein expression. Whole-genome sequencing of 3 embryos from the first patient showed that all were triploid, with an excess of maternal chromosomes. Two of the embryos were also aneuploid. Haplotype analysis indicated a meiotic origin of the triploidy: a meiosis II error in the 3PN zygote and meiosis I errors in the other 2 embryos.

paragraphs.text: Jiao et al. (2025) performed RNA sequencing on 3 day-3 embryos from a woman with compound heterozygous MEI1 mutations and compared them with control embryos. They found 2,005 downregulated and 1,904 upregulated genes. Downregulated genes were enriched in meiotic cell cycle pathways and in epigenetic regulation, including histone demethylase and deacetylase activity. Several maternal-effect genes, including FBXO43, OOEP, and WEE2, were dysregulated. From these results, the authors proposed that MEI1 dysfunction impairs both meiotic and genomic stability and the activation of the zygotic genome.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2024) studied an infertile woman with embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure. She carried a 1-bp deletion (c.3002delC) in the MEI1 gene, which they classified as a frameshift variant, together with a 16-bp deletion (c.2264_2268+11delGTGAGGTATGGACCAC). Each was inherited from a heterozygous parent. All 4 of her embryos tested were aneuploid.

paragraphs.text: In a consanguineous family, Liu et al. (2025) identified a homozygous deletion of the whole of exon 19 of the MEI1 gene. Carriers were a woman with embryonic arrest and a man with azoospermia, and their mother was heterozygous. Analysis of cDNA confirmed loss of the exon. In transfected HEK293T cells, the deletion produced a truncated protein, consistent with premature termination in exon 20.

paragraphs.text: In a 32-year-old Chinese woman with primary infertility, Jiao et al. (2025) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the MEI1 gene by whole-exome sequencing. One was a c.622T-C transition resulting in a ser208-to-pro (S208P) substitution. The other was a c.2647C-T transition resulting in an arg883-to-ter (R883X) substitution. Her fertilization was abnormal, with 3PN/PPN embryos, and her embryos were triploid with excess maternal chromosomes. Structural modeling predicted that S208P alters hydrophobic interactions. In transfected HEK293T cells, S208P did not change protein expression.

paragraphs.text: In a 35-year-old Chinese woman with primary infertility and embryonic developmental arrest, Jiao et al. (2025) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the MEI1 gene. One was a c.3037T-G transversion resulting in a trp1013-to-gly (W1013G) substitution. The other was a deletion of exons 21 to 31, given as c.2546_3525del in the text and c.2546_3825del in the table. Because the deletion spans c.3037, the patient appeared homozygous for c.3037T-G on sequencing, and qPCR confirmed the deletion. In transfected HEK293T cells, W1013G increased MEI1 protein levels, whereas the exon 21-31 deletion did not change protein expression.

agent.process_note: I read all five papers in full. Four were abstracts only (Dong 2021, Wu 2024, Liu 2025, Chen 2026); Jiao 2025 was the only full text. The papers establish MEI1 as the gene. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro gives no gene MIM number and the location is just 'chromosome 22', from the Jiao table. The abstracts of Dong 2021 and Chen 2026 do not name their variants, ancestry or family details, so no allelic variants come from those papers. Jiao 2025 is internally inconsistent: the deletion is c.2546_3525del in the text and c.2546_3825del in the table, and the oocyte counts differ between text and table. I reported the deletion discrepancy and avoided the conflicting counts. The Wu 2024 abstract says only that the two variants came from heterozygous parents; it does not explicitly state phase.
